items.stem: Describe the arrangement and movement of the particles in a liquid.
items.modelAnswer: Liquid particles are randomly arranged but still close together, moving around each other.

items.stem: State the three states of matter.
items.modelAnswer: Solids, liquids and gases.

items.stem: Explain why the same particle model can represent every substance.
items.modelAnswer: Because in the model every particle is drawn as a small solid sphere, whatever the substance — the model shows arrangement and movement, not the identity of the substance.

items.stem: Substance X has particles vibrating about fixed positions very close together; substance Y has particles far apart moving quickly in all directions. Classify each substance's state.
items.modelAnswer: X is a solid (particles sit in a regular arrangement, vibrating about fixed positions, very close together); Y is a gas (particles are randomly arranged, far apart, moving quickly in all directions).

items.stem: State what happens to the particles of a solid as it melts.
items.modelAnswer: The absorbed heat becomes kinetic energy and the particles vibrate more.

items.stem: State the relationship between the temperature at which a substance melts and the temperature at which it freezes.
items.modelAnswer: Freezing reverses melting at the same temperature — they happen at one identical temperature.

items.stem: Explain why changing state does not alter the substance's chemical identity.
items.modelAnswer: Because changing state is a physical change: the particles stay the same and only the forces between them alter.

items.stem: A student watches bubbles form throughout a heating liquid at exactly 100 °C, and sees droplets forming on a cold lid above it. State which process each observation shows.
items.modelAnswer: The bubbles forming throughout the liquid at one temperature are boiling; the droplets forming on the cold lid are condensing (condensation).

items.stem: State what eventually happens to diffusing particles left long enough.
items.modelAnswer: Given time, the particles end up evenly spread throughout the available space.

items.stem: State the energy input diffusion needs.
items.modelAnswer: None — diffusion needs no energy input (it only speeds up at higher temperatures).

items.stem: Explain why diffusion happens in gases and liquids but not in solids.
items.modelAnswer: Because diffusion requires particles in random motion — the particles of gases and liquids move randomly, while solid particles only vibrate about fixed positions.

items.stem: A drop of food colouring spreads through a beaker of cold water very slowly. State two changes that would make it spread faster.
items.modelAnswer: Warm the water — diffusion speeds up at higher temperatures — and remember liquids always diffuse slower than gases because their particles are closely packed and move slowly.

items.stem: State what dilution means.
items.modelAnswer: Dilution means adding more solvent, typically water, to an existing solution.

items.stem: State what happens to the colour of a solution with each dilution.
items.modelAnswer: The colour grows fainter with each dilution, but it does not disappear immediately.

items.stem: Explain what the lasting faint colour after many dilutions shows about a small crystal of potassium manganate(VII).
items.modelAnswer: It shows that even a small crystal must contain a huge number of tiny particles — enough to keep colouring the water after so much dilution.

items.stem: A student dilutes a solution 1:10 three times in a row. State what happens to the concentration of the solute overall.
items.modelAnswer: It falls with each dilution — adding solvent lowers the concentration of the solute particles, so after three dilutions the concentration is much lower.

items.stem: State the term for the liquid that does the dissolving.
items.modelAnswer: The solvent.

items.stem: State the units in which solubility values are recorded.
items.modelAnswer: Grams per 100 grams of solvent.

items.stem: Explain why a saturated solution of one substance can hold more dissolved solid than a saturated solution of another substance at the same temperature.
items.modelAnswer: Because different substances dissolve to different extents in the same solvent — solubility is specific to each substance.

items.stem: A diver's blood dissolves more gas at depth than at the surface. State the two trends from the note that explain more gas dissolving at depth.
items.modelAnswer: Higher pressure — gases dissolve better under high pressure — and the colder temperature deep underwater, since gases dissolve worse when warmed.

items.stem: State which salt is the exception whose solubility changes very little as temperature rises.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium chloride (NaCl).

items.stem: State what each point on a solubility curve records.
items.modelAnswer: The maximum mass that dissolves before a saturated solution forms (at that temperature).

items.stem: Explain why a solubility curve is useful once it has been drawn.
items.modelAnswer: Because reading the curve gives the mass that will dissolve at any chosen temperature, without repeating the experiment at each temperature.

items.stem: A hot saturated solution of potassium nitrate is cooled. State what you would expect to form, and why.
items.modelAnswer: Crystals form — most salts dissolve better as the water gets hotter, so cooling means the solution holds less, and the excess solid crystallises out.

items.stem: State what the leftover undissolved solid guarantees about the solution.
items.modelAnswer: It is the guarantee that the solution is saturated.

items.stem: State what may enter the pre-weighed evaporating basin.
items.modelAnswer: Only clear solution — no undissolved solid.

items.stem: Explain why this practical measures the solubility at one chosen temperature rather than across a range.
items.modelAnswer: Because solubility changes with temperature — the practical measures a solid's solubility at one chosen temperature, so the solution must be held at that temperature for the measurement to mean one clean point.

items.stem: A student weighs the dried basin once and records it immediately. State the flaw in that working, and the fix.
items.modelAnswer: One weighing may still hold water — the basin must be reheated, cooled and reweighed until two masses agree (heated to constant mass), confirming all the water has gone.

items.stem: State how the mass of the solution is obtained from the weighings.
items.modelAnswer: Mass of solution is the filled basin minus the empty basin.

items.stem: State how the solubility figure is calculated from the solid and water masses.
items.modelAnswer: The solid mass is scaled up to 100 grams of water (solid mass divided by water mass, then multiplied by 100).

items.stem: Explain why the solid mass is scaled to exactly 100 grams of water.
items.modelAnswer: Because solubility values are stated in grams per 100 grams of solvent (water), so scaling to 100 g makes the number comparable with tables and curves.

items.stem: A basin weighs 30.00 g empty, 55.00 g with solution, and 41.00 g with dry solid. State the mass of water in the sample.
State how many elements the periodic table holds.
items.modelAnswer: 118 elements (for example copper, iron and magnesium).

items.stem: State what a compound is.
items.modelAnswer: A compound joins two or more different elements by chemical bonds into one substance.

items.stem: Explain why iron sulfide, FeS, cannot be separated into iron and sulfur by sorting or magnets, while a loose mixture of the two powders can.
items.modelAnswer: Because FeS is a compound — its elements are joined by chemical bonds, and no physical method can split a compound back into the elements it contains; the loose mixture has no bonds, so physical methods separate it.

items.stem: Sample A contains only atoms with 8 protons; sample B contains atoms with 8 protons chemically bonded to atoms with 1 proton. Classify each sample.
items.modelAnswer: Sample A is an element (all its atoms hold the same number of protons); sample B is a compound (two or more different elements joined by chemical bonds).

items.stem: State what a mixture is.
items.modelAnswer: A mixture holds two or more substances in one place without chemical bonds between them.

items.stem: Name the three mixture examples the note gives.
items.modelAnswer: Sand in water, oil in water, and sulfur mixed with iron filings.

items.stem: Explain why the ingredients of a mixture can each already be compounds.
items.modelAnswer: Because the ingredients of a mixture can be elements, compounds or both at once — a mixture only needs two or more substances without chemical bonds between them, whatever each substance is.

items.stem: A student separates a mixture into its parts by evaporating the liquid away. State why physical separation was possible here but would not split a compound.
items.modelAnswer: Physical methods such as filtration or evaporation separate mixtures into their parts because mixtures have no chemical bonds between their ingredients; a compound's elements are chemically bonded, and no physical method can split it.

items.stem: State what a pure substance is in chemistry.
items.modelAnswer: A single element or a single compound, and nothing else.

items.stem: State what adding anything at all to a pure substance produces.
items.modelAnswer: A mixture — adding anything, even another pure substance, produces a mixture.

items.stem: Explain why drinking water fails the chemistry test for purity.
items.modelAnswer: Because drinking water carries dissolved ions and chlorine as well as the water molecules — a pure substance must be a single element or compound with nothing else present.

items.stem: A sealed bottle holds only nitrogen molecules. Classify the bottle's contents by the chemistry definition.
items.modelAnswer: It is pure — a single element (nitrogen), which is exactly what the chemistry definition of pure allows.

items.stem: State how a pure substance melts and boils.
items.modelAnswer: At one specific, sharp temperature (its melting point and boiling point).

items.stem: State which technique checks drug purity by heating a tiny sample slowly.
items.modelAnswer: Melting point analysis.

items.stem: Explain how melting and boiling data can distinguish a pure substance from a mixture.
items.modelAnswer: Because a pure substance melts and boils at one specific, sharp temperature while a mixture melts and boils over a range of temperatures — so a sample that melts over a range is a mixture.

items.stem: Sample A melts at 80.1 °C with a data-table value of 80.2 °C; sample B melts between 74 °C and 79 °C. State which sample is purer.
items.modelAnswer: Sample A — the closer the measured point sits to the data-table value, the purer the sample (B melts over a range, so it is a mixture).
